step1.purpose_and_description: Shouguang, a county-level township in Shandong province, China, is more important than its modest population suggests. It is among a minority of urban centers that have prospered through agriculture and agriculture-related activities when most cities in China have grown through manufacturing and/or commerce. Geography and history have combined to make Shouguang the “home of vegetables” in China. It was also agriculture that gave birth to booming secondary and services sectors. The government’s role has been crucial in upgrading value added in agriculture while strengthening infrastructure and spatial planning to facilitate urban growth. Emphasis on the latter, however, produced large-scale rural-urban migration. Land consolidation to address village “hollowout” while meeting the demand for urban expansion has been a success story. However, challenges (such as environmental and governance-related issues) remain. The Shouguang case shows that strategies promoting one sector need to take into account their likely impact on other sectors.

Shouguang, is a county-level city located in Shangdong Peninsular of northeast China (Supplementary material Fig. 1). Its coordinates are 118°32′–119°10′E and 36°41′–37°19′N. Seated at the junction of the Zihe and Yuhe Rivers, its topographical advantage has made it renowned for agriculture since ancient times. With well-developed primary industries and a good geographic location, Shouguang has also been a recipient of heavy domestic investment, contributing to its rapid industrialization.

Shouguang is a city that punches above its own weight. Although a small urban center compared to cities in China, Shouguang distinguishes itself in two respects. First, unlike many cities in China built around manufacturing e.g. Shenzhen (Ng, 2003, Wu, 1999) or commerce e.g. Shanghai (Wu, 1999), Shouguang’s growth was, and continues to be, propelled by agriculture, especially vegetable farming, which earned it the title “Home of Vegetables”. Forbes ranked Shouguang as one of the “Best Commercial Cities in Mainland China” in 2008 (“Forbes list “Best Commercial Cities in Mainland China”,” 2008), based on its achievements in agriculture. The industrialization of the city was also based on agriculture, with agricultural processing, packaging, and transportation all important industries. Shouguang has also leveraged its advantage in vegetable farming to promote agro-tourism.

With its economy straddling both rural and urban sectors, Shouguang has also become a hothouse for an important experiment in rural development. Growing prosperity in China has resulted in increased rural – urban migration on the one hand and new rural construction on the other. The effect of both is to leave rural residences unoccupied, the former because rural residents have moved and the latter because as new houses are built, old houses become vacant. This has given rise to the phenomenon of “hollowed-out” villages. The increased need for land for urban housing combined with that of greater efficiency in rural land use has given impetus to “land consolidation”, which is now a national policy. Shouguang’s success in this area has made it a model for similar efforts in other parts of China.

These special features provide the rationale for profiling Shouguang. This profile outlines the historical development and governance of the city to set the context for discussing key issues associated with urban expansion, brought about by its economic growth, giving rise to the need for infrastructural development and spatial planning, and residential land consolidation as a pragmatic response. The paper ends with a brief review of the city’s current and future challenges arising from these developments.

With well-developed primary industries and a good geographic location, Shouguang has also been a recipient of heavy domestic investment, contributing to its rapid industrialization.

Shouguang is a city that punches above its own weight. Although a small urban center compared to cities in China, Shouguang distinguishes itself in two respects. First, unlike many cities in China built around manufacturing e.g. Shenzhen (Ng, 2003, Wu, 1999) or commerce e.g. Shanghai (Wu, 1999), Shouguang’s growth was, and continues to be, propelled by agriculture, especially vegetable farming, which earned it the title “Home of Vegetables”. Forbes ranked Shouguang as one of the “Best Commercial Cities in Mainland China” in 2008 (“Forbes list “Best Commercial Cities in Mainland China”,” 2008), based on its achievements in agriculture. The industrialization of the city was also based on agriculture, with agricultural processing, packaging, and transportation all important industries. Shouguang has also leveraged its advantage in vegetable farming to promote agro-tourism.

With its economy straddling both rural and urban sectors, Shouguang has also become a hothouse for an important experiment in rural development. Growing prosperity in China has resulted in increased rural – urban migration on the one hand and new rural construction on the other. The effect of both is to leave rural residences unoccupied, the former because rural residents have moved and the latter because as new houses are built, old houses become vacant. This has given rise to the phenomenon of “hollowed-out” villages. The increased need for land for urban housing combined with that of greater efficiency in rural land use has given impetus to “land consolidation”, which is now a national policy. Shouguang’s success in this area has made it a model for similar efforts in other parts of China.

These special features provide the rationale for profiling Shouguang. This profile outlines the historical development and governance of the city to set the context for discussing key issues associated with urban expansion, brought about by its economic growth, giving rise to the need for infrastructural development and spatial planning, and residential land consolidation as a pragmatic response. The paper ends with a brief review of the city’s current and future challenges arising from these developments.

Forbes ranked Shouguang as one of the “Best Commercial Cities in Mainland China” in 2008 (“Forbes list “Best Commercial Cities in Mainland China”,” 2008), based on its achievements in agriculture. The industrialization of the city was also based on agriculture, with agricultural processing, packaging, and transportation all important industries. Shouguang has also leveraged its advantage in vegetable farming to promote agro-tourism.

With its economy straddling both rural and urban sectors, Shouguang has also become a hothouse for an important experiment in rural development. Growing prosperity in China has resulted in increased rural – urban migration on the one hand and new rural construction on the other. The effect of both is to leave rural residences unoccupied, the former because rural residents have moved and the latter because as new houses are built, old houses become vacant. This has given rise to the phenomenon of “hollowed-out” villages. The increased need for land for urban housing combined with that of greater efficiency in rural land use has given impetus to “land consolidation”, which is now a national policy. Shouguang’s success in this area has made it a model for similar efforts in other parts of China.

These special features provide the rationale for profiling Shouguang. This profile outlines the historical development and governance of the city to set the context for discussing key issues associated with urban expansion, brought about by its economic growth, giving rise to the need for infrastructural development and spatial planning, and residential land consolidation as a pragmatic response. The paper ends with a brief review of the city’s current and future challenges arising from these developments.
